case_name: Leon A. Greenblatt III & Leslie N. Jabine v. Illinois Department of Revenue
title: Leon A. Greenblatt III & Leslie N. Jabine v. Illinois Department of Revenue (19 TT 104)
text:
ILLINOIS INDEPENDENT
TAX TRIBUNAL
LEON A. GREENBLATT III & )
LESLIE N. JABINE, )
Petitioners, )
)
)
v. ) 19 TT 104
) Judge Brian F. Barov
ILLINOIS DEPARTMENT )
OF REVENUE, )
Respondent. )
ORDER ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT MOTIONS
The Illinois Income Tax Act (“IITA”) imposes a tax on individuals measured
by Illinois net income. 35 ILCS 5/201. Illinois net income is calculated, in part,
based upon the individual’s adjusted gross income, 35 ILCS 5/202, 5/203(a)(1),
“properly reportable for federal income tax purposes for the taxable year under the
provisions of the Internal Revenue Code,” 35 ILCS 5/203(e)(1). Section 506(b) of the
IITA, 35 ILC 5/506(b), requires Illinois taxpayers to report to the Illinois
Department of Revenue (“Department”) a change to federal income ‘“finally
determined for federal income tax purposes’” that affects the computation of their
Illinois net income. See Rogers v. Illinois Department of Revenue, 2017 IL App 1st
151449, ¶ 1 (quoting 35 ILCS 5/506(b)). The change must be reported by filing an
amended Illinois income tax return with the Department no later than 120 days
after the federal change is finalized. See 35 ILCS 5/506(b). The failure to make the
timely disclosure renders taxpayers liable for additional Illinois income taxes
arising from the federal tax change. See Rogers, 2017 IL App 1st 151449, ¶ 1;
Peoria & Pekin Union Railway Co. v. Department of Revenue, 301 Ill. App. 3d 736,
740-41 (3rd Dist. 1998).
1

In this case, the Department issued a Notice of Deficiency against the
Petitioners, who are individual joint income tax filers, on the ground that they
failed to report a change to their federal taxable income to the Department as
required by section 506(b). The Petitioners claim that there was no federal change
within the meaning of section 506(b), or at least not one that they knew about, and
that they were not required to file amended Illinois income tax return. The parties
have filed cross-motions for summary judgment. For the reasons explained below, I
agree with the Petitioners and find that they are entitled to summary judgment in
their favor.
Background
On March 25, 2009, after several extensions of time, the Petitioners filed
their 2007 tax year joint federal income tax return. Pet’r Ex. A, Affidavit of Leon
Greenblatt III (“Greenblatt Aff.”), at ¶ 5; Pet’r Ex. B, Affidavit of Leslie Jabine
(“Jabine Aff.”), ¶ 5.1 Thereafter, the Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) notified the
Petitioners that their 2007 federal return was under examination. See Pet’r Ex. A,
Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 9, & Pet’r Ex 1; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine Aff., at ¶ 9.2 The IRS also
1 The facts and arguments are cited as follows: Leon Greenblatt and Leslie N. Jabine’s
Motion for Summary Judgment (“Pet’r Mot.”), its exhibits (“Pet’r Ex. __”); Leon Greenblatt
III and Leslie N. Jabine’s Reply in Support of Their Motion for Summary Judgment and
Response to the Illinois Department of Revenue’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Pet’r
Response”); Leon Greenblatt III and Leslie N. Jabine’s Supplemental Brief on the Authority
to Seek a Declaration from the U.S. Tax Court (“Pet’r Supplemental Br.”); the Illinois
Department’s Motion for Summary Judgment and Response to Petitioners’ Motion for
Summary Judgment (“Dep’t Mot.”), its exhibits (“Dep’t Ex. __”); the Illinois Department of
Revenue’s Reply Brief in Support of Its Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment (“Dep’t
Reply”); the Illinois Department of Revenue’s Supplemental Response Brief in Accordance
with September 28, 2022, Order (“Dep’t Supplemental Br.”); and its Exhibits (“Dep’t
Supplemental Ex. ___”).
2 The record is not entirely clear as to when the IRS first notified the Petitioners that their
2007-2009 tax returns were under review. In their affidavits, the Petitioners both aver that
it was June 8, 2010, that they were first notified by the IRS of the audit. See Pet’r Ex. A,
Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 9; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine Aff., at ¶ 9. The power of attorney, filed by May,
however, is dated May 25, 2010, although it is stamped “received” by the local IRS office on
June 24, 2010. Pet’r Ex. C, Affidavit of Michael May (“May Aff.”), at ¶ 4-5 & May Ex. 2.
The Department refers to an April 5, 2011 letter informing the Petitioners that their 2007
federal tax return had been selected for examination as the date that the federal audit
2

began auditing the Petitioners’ 2008 and 2009 federal returns. Pet’r Ex. A,
Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 6; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine Aff. at ¶ 6. The Petitioners retained a
certified public account, Michael May (“May”), to represent them before the IRS in
the audit of the 2007, 2008 and 2009 tax years, and he filed a power of attorney on
their behalf. Pet’r Ex. C, May Affidavit, at ¶ 4. May received all communications
that the Petitioners received regarding the examination of their 2007 income tax
return. Id. at ¶ 5.
In a May 4, 2015, internal memorandum, an IRS agent stated regarding the
Petitioners’ 2007 tax year audit that, “[b]ased on review of the case file, the 2007
tax year is considered a barred statute for civil purposes.” Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt
Aff., Ex. 6. The IRS further prepared a “Statute Expiration Report” Form 3999
which referenced an amount of income tax deficiency, interest and penalties, but
checked the box that the statute expired. Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., Ex. 7. On
this Form 3999, Box No. 7, entitled “Date of Taxpayer Notification” was left blank.
Id.
The IRS further prepared a Form 5278 “Statement-Income Tax Changes.”
Dep’t Ex. 5. The Form 5278 is dated May 15, 2015 and reflected an adjustment to
federal taxable income. Id. Box 2 on the first page of this form has three check
boxes denominated “Notice of Deficiency,” “Settlement Conference,” and “Other.”
Id. None of these boxes are checked. Id. Further, Form 5278 states that “if you
agree with our examination, PLEASE SIGN PAGE 2 OF THE REPORT (Form
4549) and return pages 1 and 2 to us.” Id. The space for signing the form is blank.
Id.
The May 15, 2015, IRS Form 4549-A, “Income Tax Examination Changes
showed an adjustment to the Petitioners’ 2007 federal income. Dep’t Ex. 4. At the
top of the 4549-A form, the box entitled “Person with whom examination changes
commenced. Dep’t Mot. for Sum. J. at 2; Dep’t Ex. 2. The IRS account transcript dates the
examination of tax return from September 17, 2009 and the appointed representative as
appearing on March 2, 2010. Dep’t Ex. 6, at 2. The discrepancy in dates as to when the
federal tax audit began or when Petitioners were informed of the federal tax audit is not
material to this case; it is undisputed that they were given timely notice of the audit.
3

were discussed” is left blank. Id. The bottom of the form beneath the examiner’s
signature line, the 4549-A form provides notice that:
The Internal Revenue Service has agreements with state tax
agencies under which information about federal tax, including
increases or decreases, is exchanged with the states. If this change
affects the amount of your state income tax, you should amend your
state return by filing the necessary forms.
Id.
On December 16, 2015 the IRS issued a letter addressed to the Petitioners
regarding the 2007 tax year stating:
We are no longer examining your federal income tax return for the
period(s) listed about because the statutory period expired for us to
provide any refund or assess any deficiency.
Thank you for your cooperation.
Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 15, Ex. 4.
For the 2008 and 2009 tax years, the IRS issued the Petitioners a Notice of
Deficiency and an Explanation of the Delinquency Penalty, Form 4549-A Income
Tax Examination Changes. Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 24; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine
Aff., at ¶ 17. The Petitioners have challenged those notices in the United States
Tax Court, where they remain pending. Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 26; Pet’r
Ex. B, Jabine Aff., at ¶ 19.
The IRS never issued a determination that the Petitioners’ owed additional
sums for the for the 2007 tax year. Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff. at ¶ 25. According
to the Petitioners, and their representative May, they never received a notice of
deficiency from the IRS concerning their 2007 federal tax return or “any other
document evidencing the assessment or determination of additional tax liability”
for the 2007 tax year. Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff, at ¶ 18; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine
Aff., at ¶ 14; Pet’r Ex. C, May Aff., at ¶ 10.
As of June 19, 2017, the IRS account transcript reflected a change to the
federal adjusted gross income for the Petitioners for the tax year ending December
31, 2007. Dep’t Ex. 6, Account Transcript. However, no additional tax was
4

assessed, and no additional tax was due the federal government. Id. The
Petitioners did not report the adjustment to their income reflected on the IRS
account transcript to the Department. Dep’t Ex. 8, Affidavit of Jason Poling. On
June 19, 2019, “[b]ased on information we received from the Internal Revenue
Service,” under 26 U.S.C. 6103(d), the Department issued a notice of deficiency to
the Petitioners assessing additional Illinois income tax, interest and penalties. See
Dep’t Ex. 3. This litigation followed.
Analysis
The parties have filed cross motions for summary judgment contesting the
issue of whether the Petitioners failed to comply with section 506(b) of the IITA.
Summary judgment is proper where the pleadings, depositions, and admissions on
file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to
any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of
law. Rogers, 2017 IL App (1st), ¶ 30. Where the parties file cross-motions for
summary judgment, they invite the court to decide the case as a matter of law based
on the facts in the record. Shared Imaging, LLC v. Hamer, 2017 IL App (1st)
152817, ¶ 13. If a party moving for summary judgment supports the motion with
an affidavit or other admissible evidence that would entitle it to summary
judgment, the opposing party must provide countervailing affidavits or evidence
that raises a legitimate fact question. See Tafoya-Cruz v. Temperance Beer Co.,
2020 IL App (1st) 190606, ¶ 68; North Community Bank v. 17011 South Park Ave,
LLC, 2015 IL App (1st) 133672, ¶15. “[M]ere speculation, conjecture, or guess is
insufficient” to avoid summary judgment. Tafoya-Cruz, 2020 IL App (1st) 190606, ¶
68 (internal quotation mark omitted); Sorce v. Naperville Jeep Eagle, Inc., 309 Ill.
App. 3d 313, 329 (2d Dist. 1999).
Section 506(b) of the IITA states:
(b) Changes affecting federal income tax. A person shall notify the
Department if:
5

(1) the taxable income, any item of income or deduction, the income tax
liability, or any tax credit reported in an original or amended federal
income tax return of that person for any year or as determined by the
Internal Revenue Service or the courts is altered by amendment of
such return or as a result of any other recomputation or
redetermination of federal taxable income or loss, and such alteration
reflects a change or settlement with respect to any item or items,
affecting the computation of such person’s net income, net loss, or of any
credit provided by Article 2 of this Act for any year under this Act, or
in the number of personal exemptions allowable to such person under
Section 151 of the Internal Revenue Code.
35 ILCS 5/506(b)(emphasis added). A taxpayer is required to report any
qualifying federal change to the Department within 120 days of when the
change is “agreed to or finally determined for federal income tax purposes.”
Id.
The Petitioners’ initial argument was that they were not required to
report a federal change under section 506(b) because the IRS never issued a
Notice of Deficiency to them. See Pet’r Mot. at 5-12. The Department
responded that the reporting requirement of section 506(b) extended to any
final recomputation of federal taxable income by the IRS, even if it did not
result in a formal assessment. Dep’t Mot. at 7-11. The Department
contended that the Petitioners’ argument is flawed because it “confuses
taxable income with tax liability.” Id. at 8 (emphasis removed) (relying on
Peoria & Pekin Union Railway). Further, citing the Tribunal’s decision in
Rogers v. Illinois Department of Revenue, 14 TT153 (Apr. 27, 2015), aff’d,
2017 IL App 1st 151449, the Department argued that recording the
adjustment on the federal account transcript is evidence of its finality, thus
triggering the reporting the obligation of section 506(b). Id. at 10.
The Department’s arguments warrant a detailed discussion of these
cases. In Peoria & Pekin Union Railway, the taxpayer, a railway corporation
received a federal loan for railroad improvement projects. See 301 Ill. App. at
738. The railway did not repay the loan in full, and the federal government
6

agreed to forgive the majority of the loan. Id. The IRS audited the railway
and determined that the loan forgiveness qualified as federal taxable income
and that the railway had improperly deducted interest on the loan that it had
never paid. Id. The IRS adjusted the railway’s federal income to reflect
interest income for the 1988 tax year but never assessed the income because
the federal limitations period had expired. Id. Due to the adjustment,
however, the railway was required to recalculate certain net operating losses
and investment tax credit carryforwards for later tax years. Id.
The information regarding the federal audit was disclosed to the
Department. Id. The railway then filed amended Illinois amended income
tax returns for the 1989-1991 tax years to reflect changes in the net operating
losses and credit carryforwards for those years. Id. It also filed an amended
return for the 1988 tax year. Id. at 738-39. The 1988 amended return was
filed more than 120 days after the IRS audit findings were finalized and
stated that “[n]o change in taxable income results due to the expiration of the
statute.” Id. (internal quotes omitted).
Invoking the failure to comply with section 506(b), and after auditing
the effect of the federal changes, the Department assessed additional Illinois
income tax on the railway for the 1988 tax year arising from the federal tax
change. Id. at 739. The railway argued that its Illinois tax liability was tied
to its federal tax liability and because the IRS did not assess it additional
taxes it was not required to report the federal change under section 506(b).
Id. The Peoria & Pekin Union Railway court rejected the railway’s argument
stating:
It is change to federal taxable income that is at issue in this case
rather than tax liability. As noted above, the changes made by the IRS
did not give rise to new federal tax liability for 1988. But the federal
changes highlighted in section 506(b) are not limited to changes that
result in new federal tax liability. An alteration as stated in section
506(b) may result from an amendment or recomputation of taxable
income, changes in itemization, or changes in federal tax liability.
7

[Citations]. The action taken by the IRS was an alteration within the
scope of section 506(b) because it changed the railway’s 1988 taxable
income by increasing it $2,274,804.
Id. at 743.
Rogers was similar. There the taxpayers were married joint filers and
filed federal income tax returns reflecting partnership losses. See Rogers,
14TT153, at 1-3. The IRS audited the partnership, discovered that it had not
suffered the losses claimed and sought to collect the deficiency from the
taxpayers. Id. at 3. The husband, who was the partner in the partnership,
settled the disputed partnership losses with the IRS and signed an IRS 870-
LT form agreeing to an additional assessment, which was recorded on the
taxpayers’ account transcript. Id.
The Department then assessed a deficiency for Illinois income taxes
based on the taxpayers’ failure to provide notice of the federal change under
section 506(b). Id. at ¶ 4. The Tax Tribunal held that the settlement
agreement was an adjustment of the partnership’s return agreed to by the
partner. Id. at 12. In the alternative, this court held that the IRS transcript,
which reflected the settlement, was evidence of a final adjustment that
triggered the reporting requirement under section 506(b). Id. at 12-13. In
either case, the section 506(b) reporting requirement was triggered, and the
Department’s assessment was affirmed. Id. at 13.3
What distinguishes the present case from Peoria & Pekin Union
Railway and Rogers is that in both of those cases, the taxpayers were well
aware of the changes made to their federal income. In Peoria & Pekin Union
Railway, the 1988 federal adjustment affected the railroad’s tax return for
the 1989-1991 tax years, and the railway noted the federal adjustment on its
1988 Illinois amended returns. In Rogers, the partner-husband signed the
3 The Illinois Appellate Court affirmed the Tax Tribunal’s decision in Rogers on the ground
that the agreed settlement triggered the section 506(b) reporting requirement; it did not
reach the question of whether recording the assessment on the federal account transcript
was a final determination. See 2017 IL App (1st) 151449, at ¶ 44.
8

settlement with the IRS and the taxpayers were notified by letter of the
federal change before failing to file an amended return with the Department.
Here, there was no evidence showing that the Petitioners had notice of the
federal adjustment. The IRS Form 4549-A showed the proposed adjustment to the
Petitioners’ 2007 federal income and indicated that the IRS may report changes to
state taxing authorities. See Dep’t Ex. 4. Yet, at the top the form, the box entitled
“Person with whom examination changes were discussed” is left blank and the form
was unsigned. See id.
The IRS Form 5278 also reflected an adjustment to federal taxable income,
but was also left undated, unsigned, with no indication as to who prepared the form
and no signature or indication that the form was provided to the Petitioners. See
Dep’t Ex. 5. The Statute Expiration Report Form 3999, calculated an amount of
deficiency, interest and penalties, but space on the form titled Date of Notification
to Taxpayer is blank. See Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., Ex. 7. There was no
indication that the IRS’s May 4, 2015, internal memorandum regarding the
expiration of the statute of limitation for the Petitioners’ case was ever forwarded to
them. See Pet’r Ex. A. Greenblatt Aff., Ex. 6.
The record reflected that the only document the Petitioners received
from the IRS’s was the letter of December 16, 2015 regarding the 2007 tax
year stating:
We are no longer examining your federal income tax return for the
period(s) listed about because the statutory period expired for us to
provide any refund or assess any deficiency.
Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff., at ¶ 15, Ex. 4.
Both of the Petitioners filed affidavits that stated that they never
received a notice of deficiency from the IRS concerning their 2007 federal
tax return or “any other document evidencing the assessment or
determination of additional tax liability” for the 2007 tax year. Pet’r Ex. A,
Greenblatt Aff, at 18; Pet’r Ex. B, Jabine Aff., at 14. May, their
9

accountant and representative before the IRS, stated similarly in his
affidavit. Pet’r Ex. C, May Aff., at 10. Even acknowledging that this
testimony is limited to notice of a federal assessment and did not address
federal notification of an adjustment, the Department has not come
forward with any facts to show that notice of a federal change was
provided to the Petitioners.
In fact, the Department did not sharply contest the fact that the
IRS did not give the Petitioners notice of the adjustment to federal
adjusted gross income in either its summary judgment filings or at oral
argument. Rather, the Department contended that the June 19, 2019,
Notice of Deficiency was proper notice of the IRS recomputation because
the Petitioners could (and still can) challenge the IRS’s federal tax
adjustment under either federal law, or under the IITA in the Tax
Tribunal, but have not attempted to do so.
The parties were granted leave to provide supplemental authority
on the issue of whether the “the Petitioners had or have the right or ability
to challenge or recompute the adjustment to their 2007 taxable or adjusted
gross income reflected on the IRS account transcript submitted as
Department Exhibit 6 in this case.” See Leon A Greenblatt & Leslie N Jabine
v. Department of Revenue, 19TT104, Doc. 44, Order 92822. As to a federal
remedy, the Department supplied a copy of IRS brochures outlining the
federal taxpayer’s rights generally, see Dep’t Supplemental Br. Ex. 1 and
appeal rights, Dep’t Supplemental Br. Ex. 2. Neither publication
identified any vehicle to reopen an audit question at the federal level
when no additional liability is assessed for the tax year in question. And,
as the Petitioners point out, see Pet’r Supplemental Br. at 3-5, they had
no standing to challenge the adjustment that did not result in additional
liability in federal tax court, see, e.g., MacDonald v. Commissioner, 2009
Tax Ct. Memo LEXIS 242 (Oct. 22, 2009) (holding that absent a new tax
10

liability to collect by the IRS, there is no justiciable case or controversy in
federal tax court).
The Department emphasized two sources of authority under state law to
challenge the IRS adjustment. First, the Department cites regulation
100.9200(a)(4), which states regarding the section 506(b)-reporting
requirement:
Thus, it shall be the Department’s position and practice to rely upon
and accept the federal Internal Revenue Service determination as to
the amount of a taxpayer's adjusted gross or taxable income and the
number of exemptions to which he is entitled for federal income tax
purposes. Adherence to that position shall be subject to exception only
in rare circumstances such as where the Internal Revenue Service for
some reason (e.g., where no change in federal tax liability would result)
might fail or decline to act, or where the 18-month statutory period of
limitations for prosecution would expire before action by IRS.
86 Ill. Adm. Code 100.9200(a)(4) (emphasis added).
The italicized language of rule 100.9200(a)(4) does not apply here. The first
clause of the above highlighted language is inapplicable because this case is not
the “rare” circumstance in which “no change in federal tax liability would result.”
Had the IRS acted within the limitations period, its adjustment would have
affected the Petitioners’ federal tax liability. See Pet’r Ex. A, Greenblatt Aff.,
Ex. 7; Dep’t Exs. 4& 5. As for the second highlighted clause, the Department
never explained what the “18-month statutory period of limitations for
prosecution” referred to (the statute of limitations at the federal level presumably
was 26 USCS § 6501, which provides a three-year limitation on federal tax
assessments). Given that the highlighted language does not apply, the operative
language of section 100.9200(a)(4) is that the Department would “accept the IRS’s
determinations as to amounts of gross or taxable income.” Peoria & Pekin Union
Railway, 301 Ill. App. 3d at 742. Rule 100.9200(a)(4) does not support the
Department’s argument.
Last, the Department argued that the language of section 203(e)(1) of the IITA,
which states generally that the computation of Illinois net income starts with
11

adjusted income “properly reportable for federal income tax purposes for the taxable
year under the provisions of the Internal Revenue Code,” 35 ILCS 5/203(e)(1), can
be construed to permit the Petitioners to challenge a final IRS computation of
federal adjusted gross income in the Tribunal. Illinois courts may interpret federal
law and regulations to determine how they interact with state tax provisions in
order decided a question of state taxation. See Bodine Electric Co. v. Allphin, 81 Ill.
502, 511-12 (1980); AT&T Teleholdings, Inc. v. Department of Revenue, 2012 IL App
(1st) 113053, ¶ 63. But the Department’s position goes well beyond that principle.
It contends that this court should act as a federal tax tribunal to decide whether the
IRS correctly construed and applied federal law.
The Department’s arguments fly in the face of the arguments it advanced here,
see Dep’t Mot. at 10; Dep’t Reply at 6-7, and accepted by the Tribunal in Rogers,
14TT153, at 12-13, that the federal account transcript is evidence of a final
determination for federal tax purposes. Moreover, under the IITA, a taxpayer’s
calculation of Illinois net income starts with the taxpayer’s federal calculation of
gross income. See Bodine Electric Co., 81 Ill. 2d at 512; Rockwood Holding Co. v.
Department of Revenue, 312 Ill. App. 3d 1120, 1124 (1st Dist. 2000). This principle
that the calculation of state and federal incomes should conform with each other
was “intended to simplify tax computation and to develop some degree of
consistency in Federal and State income reporting.” Bodine Electric Co. v. Allphin,
81 Ill. 2d 512. The administrative, compliance and reliance interests of conformity
will be lost if taxpayers or the Department could relitigate the IRS’s final
determinations of adjusted gross income under the IITA. See, e.g., Wendy’s
International, Inc. v. Hamer, 2013 IL App (4th) 110678, ¶¶ 38-39 (upholding
conformity between federal and state tax definitions of insurance companies).
Section 203(e)(1) cannot be construed to allow parties to challenge the IRS’s
final determination under 506(b) of the IITA.
Due process requires notice and an opportunity to be heard before a tax
liability “becomes finally established.” Little Sister Coal Corp. v. Dawson 45 Ill. 2d
12

342, 348 (1970) (citing Dietman v. Hunter, 5 Ill. 2d 486, 489 (1955)). The failure to
do so “renders the tax void and uncollectible.” Dietman, 5 Ill. 2d at 489.
Here, the Petitioners have shown that they did not receive notice of the
federal government’s adjustment to their federal income and had no opportunity
to challenge that adjustment. I must underscore that the lack of notice was not
the fault of the Department–it acted properly in issuing the Notice of Deficiency
based on the information received from the IRS. The present case offers an
anomalous instance in which the federal government erred, but the burden of that
error must be borne by the Department. As the Petitioners have shown that they
never had notice and an opportunity to be heard on the IRS’s adjustment, the
Department’s notice of deficiency must be vacated.
Conclusion
The Petitioner’s motion for summary judgment is GRANTED. The
Department’s cross-motion for summary judgment is DENIED. The Department’s
notice of deficiency is cancelled, vacated and penalties are abated.
This is a final order subject to appeal under section 3-113 of the
Administrative Review Law, and service by email is service under section 3-113(a).
See 35 ILCS 1010/1-90; 86 Ill. Admn. Code § 5000.330. The Tribunal is a necessary
party to this appeal.
_s/ Brian Barov_________
BRIAN F. BAROV
Administrative Law Judge
Date: November 14, 2022
